To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

China has a lower level of civic involvement and higher level of neighbourhood trust, compared with Britain; that the two countries have a similar degree of class effects in civic involvement, but a greater degree of class effect in neighbourhood trust in Britain; and that the differences in civic involvement and neighbourhood trust between China and Britain can be explained mainly by the structural differences between the two countries.

(1) there is a greater difference in social trust across the social classes in Britain than in China, but a greater difference in civic engagement in Britain than in the latter, (2) the class differences in social trust in China are small, while those in civic engagement in the two countries are similar, (3) the class differences are more pronounced than the demographic effects in both social trust and civic engagement, and (4) the demographic effects are similar in the two countries

China and Britain have similar class effects in civic engagement but different class effects in neighbourhood trust, and that class plays a major role both in the development of civic engagement and in the development of neighbourhood trust.
In summary, our research is concerned with
class effects on the development of social trust and social capital.
the social class differences in social capital, and how these differences vary in different societies.
the relationship between social class and social capital.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there are more similarities than differences between the two countries in the class effects on social capital.
class differences are more significant than differences in social capital in Britain and China.
social capital in China is not as strong as in Britain, but it is not weaker than Britain in all respects.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the two countries are very different in their social structures, but very similar in their class structures and class effects on civic engagement and social capital.
class differences in civic engagement and social capital are more pronounced in Britain than in China, but the two societies are not very different in this respect.
the class differences in civic engagement are similar between China and Britain, but class differences in neighbourhood trust are more prominent in Britain.
The main takeaway from our work is that
social class matters for social capital, but it is the specific class structure that matters more.
social capital in the two countries is shaped by different institutional arrangements and demographic characteristics.
social class is a key factor in the development of both civic engagement and neighbourhood social trust.
